claim: The rose-grain aphid Metopolophium dirhodum is one of the most common and economically important aphid pests of cereals, including wheat, barley, rye, and oat, worldwide.
source: The rose-grain aphid, Metopolophium dirhodum (Walker) (Hemiptera: Aphididae), is one of the most common and economically important aphid pests of cereals, including wheat, barley, rye, and oat, worldwide (Cannon, 1986; Honěk, 1991; Ma et al., 2004; Li et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Cannon, 1986; Honěk, 1991; Ma et al., 2004; Li et al., 2020a).

claim: M. dirhodum is native in the Holarctic and then introduced into South America, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand.
source: M. dirhodum is native in the Holarctic and then introduced into South America, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand (Martinkova et al., 2018; Blackman and Eastop, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Martinkova et al., 2018; Blackman and Eastop, 2000).

claim: Under the continental climate of Central Europe, M. dirhodum is usually the most abundant aphid species on cereals.
source: Under the continental climate of Central Europe, M. dirhodum is usually the most abundant aphid species on cereals (Martinkova et al., 2018; Honěk, 1987; Praslicka, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Martinkova et al., 2018; Honěk, 1987; Praslicka, 1996).

claim: In China, M. dirhodum was first recorded in the 1980s and then gradually spread from the western to eastern side of the wheat-growing regions, resulting in increased crop yield reduction.
source: In China, M. dirhodum was first recorded in the 1980s and then gradually spread from the western to eastern side of the wheat-growing regions, resulting in increased crop yield reduction (Gong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Gong et al., 2021).

claim: M. dirhodum damages cereals by sucking the juice from wheat leaves, stems, and young ears, further resulting in the deterioration of plant nutrition.
source: M. dirhodum damages cereals by sucking the juice from wheat leaves, stems, and young ears, further resulting in the deterioration of plant nutrition (Holt et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Holt et al., 1984).

claim: M. dirhodum defecates sticky honeydew that further obstructs photosynthesis and reduces wheat quality.
source: This aphid defecates sticky honeydew that further obstructs photosynthesis and reduces wheat quality (Jiang et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jiang et al., 2019).

claim: M. dirhodum transmits a number of pathogenic plant viruses, including the barley yellow dwarf virus.
source: and transmits a number of pathogenic plant virus, including the barley yellow dwarf virus (Kennedy and Connery, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kennedy and Connery, 2005).

claim: The nymphs and adults of M. dirhodum may cause yield losses of 27–30% during the latter part of flowering stages of wheat.
source: The nymphs and adults of this aphid may cause yield losses of 27–30% during the latter part of flowering stages of wheat (Holt et al., 1984; Sánchez Chopa and Descamps, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Holt et al., 1984; Sánchez Chopa and Descamps, 2012).

claim: Wing polymorphism is commonly observed in insects of various orders, including Hemiptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Orthoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Isoptera, Psocoptera, and Dermaptera.
source: Wing polymorphism is commonly observed in insects of various orders, including Hemiptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Orthoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Isoptera, Psocoptera, and Dermaptera (Zhang et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2019a).

claim: M. dirhodum can produce wing morphs when exposed to crowding, poor nutrition, and temperature or photoperiod changes.
source: Similar to most aphids, M. dirhodum can produce wing morphs when exposed to crowding, poor nutrition, and temperature or photoperiod changes (Müller et al., 2001; Braendle et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Müller et al., 2001; Braendle et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2019b).

claim: Wingless morphs allocate additional resources to reproduction, enabling rapid colony growth.
source: In particular, wingless morphs allocate additional resources to reproduction, enabling rapid colony growth.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Winged morphs focus on dispersal, which enables them to look for new habitats and food resources.
source: Meanwhile, winged morphs focus on dispersal, which enables them to look for new habitats and food resources.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Compared with wingless ones, winged morphs are better at long-distance migration and host alternation, thus causing more serious host damage and virus transmission.
source: Compared with wingless ones, winged morphs are better at long-distance migration and host alternation, thus causing more serious host damage and virus transmission (Zhang et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zhang et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2019b).

claim: Transcription factors Zfh1 and FoxO regulate alternative wing morphs by faithfully relaying the insulin signaling activity in Nilaparvata lugens.
source: Transcription factors, Zfh1 and FoxO, were verified to regulate alternative wing morphs by faithfully relaying the insulin signaling activity in Nilaparvata lugens, providing a new dimension to the molecular explanations of this unique feature in insects (Xu et al., 2015; Xu and Zhang, 2017; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Xu et al., 2015; Xu and Zhang, 2017; Lin et al., 2016).

claim: miR-34 regulates wing dimorphism by mediating the cross-talk among insulin signaling pathway, 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), and juvenile hormone in a positive feedback manner in N. lugens.
source: Furthermore, miR-34 could regulate wing dimorphism by mediating the cross-talk among insulin signaling pathway, 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), and juvenile hormone in a positive feedback manner in N. lugens (Ye et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ye et al., 2019).

claim: Aphids and planthoppers may develop two different strategies in wing dimorphism.
source: Aphids and planthoppers may develop two different strategies in wing dimorphism.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on the differences described in the text.

claim: Planthopper nymphs can respond to environmental cues to develop into long- or short-winged morphs.
source: Planthopper nymphs can respond to environmental cues to develop into long- or short-winged morphs (Zhang et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2019a).

claim: Wing polymorphism in aphids is usually transgenerational, where the parthenogenetic mother could produce either winged or wingless offspring in response to different environmental factors.
source: Meanwhile, wing polymorphism in aphids is usually transgenerational. The parthenogenetic mother could produce either winged or wingless offspring in response to different environmental factors (Brisson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Brisson et al., 2010).

claim: A relatively high number of wingless offspring were produced after treatment with 20E or its analogue.
source: Vellichirammal et al., 2017 observed that a relatively high number of wingless offspring were produced after treatment with 20E or its analogue.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Vellichirammal et al., 2017).

claim: Many winged offspring were produced when ecdysone signaling was suppressed by RNA interference (RNAi) targeting the ecdysone receptor (EcR).
source: Conversely, many winged offspring were produced when ecdysone signaling was suppressed by RNA interference (RNAi) targeting the ecdysone receptor (EcR) (Vellichirammal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Vellichirammal et al., 2017).

claim: Elevated maternal ecdysone signaling may suppress the embryonic insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IIS) signaling and result in the high expression of FoxO-targeted genes for producing wingless offspring.
source: A hypothesized model suggested that the elevated maternal ecdysone signaling may suppress the embryonic insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IIS) signaling and result in the high expression of FoxO-targeted genes for producing wingless offspring; the opposite is true for producing winged offspring (Grantham et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Grantham et al., 2020) and is described as a hypothesized model.

claim: 20E is an essential regulatory factor underlying transgenerational plasticity in wing-dimorphic aphid.
source: These results indicated that 20E is an essential regulatory factor underlying transgenerational plasticity in wing-dimorphic aphid.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the results described in the preceding text.

claim: Adenosine (A) to inosine (I) editing is the most prevalent type of RNA post-transcriptional modification catalyzed by adenosine deaminase (ADAR) that uses double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) as substrate.
source: Adenosine (A) to inosine (I) editing is the most prevalent type of RNA post-transcriptional modification catalyzed by adenosine deaminase (adenosine deaminase acting on RNA [ADAR]) that uses double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) as substrate.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cellular machineries usually recognize inosine (I) as guanosine (G) during translation owing to the highly similar structures of I and G.
source: Owing to the highly similar structures of I and guanosine (G), cellular machineries usually recognize I as G during translation (Duan et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Duan et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2017).

claim: High-throughput sequencing has greatly facilitated the genome-wide identification of RNA-editing events.
source: High-throughput sequencing has greatly facilitated the genome-wide identification of RNA-editing events, and A-to-I RNA-editing sites have been systematically characterized in various organisms, such as humans (Picardi et al., 2017), macaques (An et al., 2019), mice, (Licht et al., 2019), worms (Rajendren et al., 2021), and cephalopods (Liscovitch-Brauer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Picardi et al., 2017; An et al., 2019; Licht et al., 2019; Rajendren et al., 2021; Liscovitch-Brauer et al., 2017).

claim: A-to-I RNA-editing sites have been systematically characterized in humans, macaques, mice, worms, and cephalopods.
source: High-throughput sequencing has greatly facilitated the genome-wide identification of RNA-editing events, and A-to-I RNA-editing sites have been systematically characterized in various organisms, such as humans (Picardi et al., 2017), macaques (An et al., 2019), mice, (Licht et al., 2019), worms (Rajendren et al., 2021), and cephalopods (Liscovitch-Brauer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Picardi et al., 2017; An et al., 2019; Licht et al., 2019; Rajendren et al., 2021; Liscovitch-Brauer et al., 2017).

claim: A high-quality reference genome of M. dirhodum was generated in this work.
source: In this work, we generated a high-quality reference genome of M. dirhodum and performed transcriptome analyses to systematically identify the A-to-I RNA-editing sites of all transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Transcriptome analyses were performed to systematically identify the A-to-I RNA-editing sites of all transcripts in M. dirhodum.
source: In this work, we generated a high-quality reference genome of M. dirhodum and performed transcriptome analyses to systematically identify the A-to-I RNA-editing sites of all transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Two synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing sites on CYP18A1 were identified to be closely associated with transgenerational wing dimorphism induced by crowding.
source: The A-to-I mRNA-editing events of numerous genes in 20E biosynthesis and signaling were examined, and two synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing sites on CYP18A1 were identified to be closely associated with transgenerational wing dimorphism induced by crowding.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: CYP18A1 plays key roles in 20E metabolism, and its abnormal expression could significantly change the 20E titer, resulting in developmental disorders in multiple insect species.
source: CYP18A1 plays key roles in 20E metabolism, and its abnormal expression could significantly change the 20E titer, resulting in developmental disorders in multiple insect species (Guittard et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Guittard et al., 2011).

claim: One synonymous A-to-I mRNA-editing site may change the binding ability of miR-3036-5p to CYP18A1, thus affecting the CYP18A1 expression, 20E metabolism, and wing dimorphism of offspring in M. dirhodum.
source: Furthermore, we identified that one synonymous A-to-I mRNA-editing site may change the binding ability of miR-3036-5p to CYP18A1, thus affecting the CYP18A1 expression, 20E metabolism, and wing dimorphism of offspring in M. dirhodum.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: A-to-I RNA editing is a dynamic mechanism in the regulation of transgenerational wing dimorphism in aphids.
source: These findings support that A-to-I RNA editing is a dynamic mechanism in the regulation of transgenerational wing dimorphism in aphids and would advance our understanding of the roles of RNA editing in environmental adaptability and phenotypic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the findings described in the manuscript.

claim: A total of 41.17 Gb of high-quality paired-end reads were obtained by Illumina genomic sequencing (~92.22× coverage).
source: A total of 41.17 Gb of high-quality paired-end reads were obtained by Illumina genomic sequencing (~92.22× coverage, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the sequencing data generated in the study.

claim: The genome size of M. dirhodum was estimated to be 457.2 M based on k-mer counting.
source: The genome size of M. dirhodum was estimated to be 457.2 M based on k-mer counting.
evidence: The claim is supported by the k-mer analysis performed in the study.

claim: k-mer distribution analysis revealed a peak at 79.8× of the sequencing depth that suggested a moderate level of heterozygosity (0.445%) and highly repetitive sequence content (59.20%) in the genome.
source: k-mer distribution analysis revealed a peak at 79.8× of the sequencing depth that suggested a moderate level of heterozygosity (0.445%) and highly repetitive sequence content (59.20%) in the genome (Figure 1A), similar to those in other Aphidinae insects with low or moderate level of heterozygosity (Jiang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the k-mer analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 1A, and compared to published literature (Jiang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019a).

claim: 161.53 Gb of PacBio long reads were generated using a CCS model.
source: To obtain a reference genome for M. dirhodum, we generated 161.53 Gb of PacBio long reads using a CCS model (Supplementary file 1) and subsequently corrected them into 10.34 Gb HiFi reads.
evidence: The claim is supported by the sequencing data generated in the study.

claim: The genome was initially assembled using hifiasm, resulting in 296 contigs with a contig N50 of 7.82 Mb and the longest contig of 23.64 Mb.
source: The genome was initially assembled using hifiasm, resulting in 296 contigs with a contig N50 of 7.82 Mb and the longest contig of 23.64 Mb (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the assembly results shown in Table 1.

claim: The 41.17 Gb of short reads generated by Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform were mapped against the assembly, resulting in a mapping rate of 92.18%.
source: The 41.17 Gb of short reads generated by Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform were then mapped against our assembly, resulting in a mapping rate of 92.18%.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mapping analysis performed in the study.

claim: BUSCO analysis showed that 96.9% (single-copied gene: 92.5%; duplicated gene: 4.4%) of the 1367 single-copy genes in the insecta_odb10 database were identified as complete, 0.4% were fragmented, and 2.7% were missing in the assembled genome.
source: BUSCO analysis showed that 96.9% (single-copied gene: 92.5%; duplicated gene: 4.4%) of the 1367 single-copy genes in the insecta_odb10 database were identified as complete, 0.4% were fragmented, and 2.7% were missing in the assembled genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by the BUSCO analysis performed in the study.

claim: The percentage of complete single-copy genes in M. dirhodum is higher than those in the genomes of Sitobion miscanthi (90.2%), Rhopalosiphum maidis (94.5%), Acyrthosiphon pisum (93.5%), and Eriosoma lanigerum (96.8%).
source: The percentage of complete single-copy genes is higher than those in the genomes of some other insect species, such as Sitobion miscanthi (90.2%) (Jiang et al., 2019), Rhopalosiphum maidis (94.5%) (Chen et al., 2019a), Acyrthosiphon pisum (93.5%) (International Aphid Genomics Consortium, 2010), and Eriosoma lanigerum (96.8%) (Biello et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing the BUSCO results to published literature (Jiang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019a; International Aphid Genomics Consortium, 2010; Biello et al., 2021).

claim: A total of 38.09 Gb of clean reads (150 bp paired-end) were obtained from the Hi-C library (coverage: 85.31×).
source: For the chromosome-level assembly, 38.09 Gb of clean reads (150 bp paired-end) were obtained from the Hi-C library (coverage: 85.31×, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the Hi-C sequencing data generated in the study.

claim: A total of 118,367,396 (86.83%) reads were mapped to the draft genome.
source: A total of 118,367,396 (86.83%) reads were mapped to the draft genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Hi-C mapping analysis performed in the study.

claim: Among the Hi-C sequences, 96,331,684 (70.67%) were uniquely mapped and then analyzed with 3D-DNA software to assist genomic assembly.
source: Among these sequences, 96,331,684 (70.67%) were uniquely mapped and then analyzed with 3D-DNA software to assist genomic assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Hi-C mapping and assembly analysis performed in the study.

claim: Sixty-eight scaffolds were assembled with an N50 length of 37.54 Mb.
source: Sixty-eight scaffolds were assembled with an N50 length of 37.54 Mb (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the assembly results shown in Table 1.

claim: 447.8 Mb genomic sequences (accounting for 98.50% of the whole assembled length) were located on nine chromosomes.
source: Finally, 447.8 Mb genomic sequences (accounting for 98.50% of the whole assembled length) were located on nine chromosomes (Figure 1B, Table 1, Supplementary file 2), which is identical to S. miscanthi (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by the assembly results shown in Figure 1B and Table 1, and compared to published literature (Jiang et al., 2019).

claim: The contig N50 and scaffold N50 of M. dirhodum were higher than those of previously reported aphid genome assemblies.
source: The contig N50 and scaffold N50 of M. dirhodum were also higher than those of previously reported aphid genome assemblies (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing the assembly statistics in Table 1 to previously reported aphid genomes.

claim: This is the first high-quality chromosome-level genome of M. dirhodum.
source: This is the first high-quality chromosome-level genome of M. dirhodum, which will be very helpful for the cloning, functional verification, and evolutionary analysis of genes in this important species or even other Hemiptera insects.
evidence: The claim is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: 34.97% of the M. dirhodum genome was annotated as repeat sequences.
source: In total, 34.97% of the M. dirhodum genome was annotated as repeat sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by the repeat annotation analysis performed in the study.

claim: Long terminal repeats (LTRs), long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs), and DNA transposons accounted for 9.23%, 2.25%, and 10.33% of the whole genome, respectively.
source: Long terminal repeats (LTRs), long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs), and DNA transposons accounted for 9.23%, 2.25%, and 10.33% of the whole genome, respectively, and 13.16% of repeat sequences were annotated as unclassified.
evidence: The claim is supported by the repeat annotation analysis performed in the study.

claim: A total of 286 tRNAs were predicted by trnascan-SE.
source: A total of 286 tRNAs were predicted by trnascan-SE.
evidence: The claim is supported by the tRNA prediction analysis performed in the study.

claim: Using infernal, 51 small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), 586 ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs), 73 small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs), 59 microRNAs (miRNAs), 286 tRNAs, and 639 other types of ncRNAs were identified.
source: Using infernal, we also identified 51 small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), 586 ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs), 73 small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs), 59 microRNAs (miRNAs), 286 tRNAs, and 639 other types of ncRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ncRNA prediction analysis performed in the study.

claim: 18,003 protein-coding genes with a mean CDS length of 1776 bp were identified from the M. dirhodum genome.
source: After repeat sequences were masked, 18,003 protein-coding genes with a mean CDS length of 1776 bp were identified from the M. dirhodum genome using de novo, homology-, and RNA sequencing-based methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by the gene prediction analysis performed in the study.

claim: The number of genes in the M. dirhodum genome is comparable with that of several other Aphidinae species, such as S. miscanthi with 16,006 protein-coding genes and Diuraphis noxia with 19,097 protein-coding genes.
source: The number of genes in the M. dirhodum genome is comparable with that of several other Aphidinae species, such as S. miscanthi with 16,006 protein-coding genes (Jiang et al., 2019) and Diuraphis noxia with 19,097 protein-coding genes (Nicholson et al., 2015), but far less than those of R. maidis (Chen et al., 2019a), A. pisum (International Aphid Genomics Consortium, 2010), Myzus persicae (Jiang et al., 2013), and E. lanigerum (Biello et al., 2021) with 26,286, 36,195, 23,910, and 28,186 protein-coding genes, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing the gene count to published literature (Jiang et al., 2019; Nicholson et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019a; International Aphid Genomics Consortium, 2010; Jiang et al., 2013; Biello et al., 2021) and shown in Table 1.

claim: Functional annotation found that 16,548 (91.92%), 9030 (50.16%), and 12,836 (71.30%) genes had significant hits with the proteins catalogued in NR, SwissProt, and eggNOG, respectively.
source: Functional annotation found that 16,548 (91.92%), 9030 (50.16%), and 12,836 (71.30%) genes had significant hits with the proteins catalogued in NR, SwissProt, and eggNOG, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by the functional annotation analysis performed in the study.

claim: A total of 9260 (51.44%) and 6254 (34.74%) genes were annotated to GO terms and KEGG pathway, respectively.
source: A total of 9260 (51.44%) and 6254 (34.74%) genes were annotated to GO terms and KEGG pathway, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the functional annotation analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of 209,881 genes were assigned to 22,945 orthogroups for the 10 species.
source: A total of 209,881 genes were assigned to 22,945 orthogroups for the 10 species (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the orthology analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: M. dirhodum and the five other Aphididae insects formed an Aphididae cluster, showing that M. dirhodum is close to A. pisum but separated from M. sacchari and R. maidis.
source: M. dirhodum and the five other Aphididae insects formed an Aphididae cluster, showing that M. dirhodum is close to A. pisum but separated from M. sacchari and R. maidis (Chen et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis performed in the study and compared to published literature (Chen et al., 2019a).

claim: The syntenic relationships between M. dirhodum and A. pisum genome reveal high levels of genome rearrangement between the chromosomes and a number of fission and fusion events.
source: The syntenic relationships between M. dirhodum and A. pisum genome were compared. The results reveal high levels of genome rearrangement between the chromosomes of M. dirhodum and A. pisum and a number of fission and fusion events (International Aphid Genomics Consortium, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by the synteny analysis performed in the study and compared to published literature (International Aphid Genomics Consortium, 2010).

claim: Chr1 in M. dirhodum shares 81.9% of the syntenic blocks of chr X in A. pisum, indicating that chr 1 might be the sex chromosome in M. dirhodum.
source: Chr1 in M. dirhodum shares 81.9% of the syntenic blocks of chr X in A. pisum (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 4), indicating that chr 1 might be the sex chromosome in M. dirhodum (Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the synteny analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 1C, and compared to published literature (Li et al., 2020b).

claim: A total of 11,678 A-to-I RNA-editing sites were obtained in M. dirhodum.
source: After processing, a total of 11,678 A-to-I RNA-editing sites were obtained in M. dirhodum (Supplementary file 5), of which 1557 are located on chromosome-1, 1397 on chromosome-2, 1472 on chromosome-3, 1300 on chromosome-4, 1257 on chromosome-5, 898 on chromosome-6, 1300 on chromosome-7, 1197 on chromosome-8, 1299 on chromosome-9, and 1 on scaffold 30 (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-editing analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Among the A-to-I RNA-editing sites, 4356 (37.3%) are in intergenic regions, and 7323 (62.7%) in 3090 protein-coding genes.
source: Among the A-to-I RNA-editing sites, 4356 (37.3%) are in intergenic regions, and 7323 (62.7%) in 3090 protein-coding genes, 342 (2.9%) in 5ʹ UTRs, 4515 (38.7%) in introns, and 466 (4.0%) in 3ʹ UTRs; 515 (4.4%) are nonsynonymous (in CDS regions and causes amino acid changes when edited) and 1485 (12.7%) are synonymous (in CDS regions but do not cause amino acid changes) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-editing analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average level of editing sites on chromosome-1 to -9 ranges from 57.2% to 59.3%, showing only a marginal difference.
source: The average level of these editing sites on chromosome-1 to -9 ranges from 57.2% to 59.3%, showing only a marginal difference (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-editing analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The A-to-I RNA-editing density of chromosome-1 (the sex chromosome, chromosome-X) is lower than those of the other eight chromosomes.
source: Given the different lengths of the nine assembled chromosomes, the A-to-I RNA-editing density of chromosome-1 (the sex chromosome, chromosome-X) is lower than those of the other eight chromosomes (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-editing analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 20E is an essential control factor underlying transgenerational plasticity in wing-dimorphic aphids.
source: 20E is an essential control factor underlying transgenerational plasticity in wing-dimorphic aphids. An environmentally regulated maternal ecdysteroid hormone can mediate wing dimorphism in the next generation (Vellichirammal et al., 2017; Vellichirammal et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Vellichirammal et al., 2017; Vellichirammal et al., 2016).

claim: The A-to-I RNA editing of numerous genes in 20E biosynthesis and signaling pathway, including CYP306A1, CYP302A1, CYP315A1, CYP18A1, ECR, FTZ-F1, and E74, was identified.
source: The A-to-I RNA editing of numerous genes in 20E biosynthesis and signaling pathway (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 6; Luan et al., 2013), including CYP306A1, CYP302A1, CYP315A1, CYP18A1, ECR, FTZ-F1, and E74, was identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by the RNA-editing analysis performed in the study and shown in Figure 3A, and compared to published literature (Luan et al., 2013).

claim: Crowding of the parent (100 mother aphids in a 10 cm3 tube) increased the winged offspring by 36.4% compared with that under normal conditions (10 mother aphids in a 10 cm3 tube).
source: Transgenerational wing dimorphism was observed in M. dirhodum in which crowding of the parent (100 mother aphids in a 10 cm3 tube) increased the winged offspring (a total of 255 offspring were used to calculate the proportion of winged and wingless individuals in the crowding group, n=255) by 36.4% (Figure 3E) compared with that under normal conditions (10 mother aphids in a 10 cm3 tube) (n=277).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 20E treatment for the crowded parent significantly decreased the number of winged offspring by 31.2%.
source: Nevertheless, 20E treatment for the crowded parent significantly decreased the number of winged offspring (n=272) by 31.2% (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The proportions of two synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing sites (editing site 528 and 759) on CYP18A1 were significantly higher in the parents treated with crowding (93.3% and 36.4%) and crowding + 20E (86.6% and 35.6%) than those in the normal group (21.3% and 20.0%).
source: The proportions of two synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing sites (editing site 528 and 759, the 528th and 759th nucleotide in the CDS region of CYP18A1) (Figure 3C and D) on CYP18A1 were significantly higher in the parents treated with crowding (93.3% and 36.4%) and crowding + 20E (86.6% and 35.6%) than those in the normal group (21.3% and 20.0%) (RNA extraction was individually performed from 150 aphids and then used for reverse transcription and gene amplification in normal, crowding, and crowding + 20E groups) (Figure 3F).
